(The power supply for the lamp is not shown.)

[Diagram: semiconductor device connected to a millivoltmeter (mV); a lamp at distance $d$ from the device]

(a) Outline why the student has recorded the $\varepsilon$ values to different numbers of significant digits but the same number of decimal places. [2]

(b) The graph shows some of the data points with the uncertainty in the $d$ values.
On the graph
(i) draw the data point corresponding to the value of $d = 19.1$ cm. [1]
(ii) assuming that there is a constant absolute uncertainty in measuring all values of $d$, draw the error bar for the data point in (b)(i). [1]
(iii) sketch the line of best-fit for all the plotted points. [1]

B1. This question is in two parts. Part 1 is about electromagnetic induction. Part 2 is about nuclear fusion.

Part 1 Electromagnetic induction

(a) A bar magnet falls vertically from rest through a coil of wire. The potential difference (pd) across the coil is recorded by a datalogger.
[Diagram: magnet falling towards a coil connected to a datalogger]
The graph shows the variation with time of the pd across the coil.
[Graph: pd / V (−0.8 to 0.8) against time / s (0 to 1.3); negative pulse to about −0.6 V near 0.33 s, then positive pulse to 0.8 V near 0.45 s, zero otherwise]
(i) Explain, with reference to Faraday's and Lenz's laws, the shape of the graph. [3]
(ii) The coil has 1500 turns. Calculate the magnitude of the maximum rate of change of magnetic flux. [3]

(b) The magnet is now suspended from a spring. The magnet is displaced vertically and starts to oscillate in and out of the coil. A sinusoidal alternating current of rms value 280 nA is induced in the coil.
(i) State in words how the rms value of the alternating current relates to a direct current of 280 nA. [1]
(ii) The coil has a resistance of 1.5 MΩ. Calculate the peak voltage across the coil. [2]
(iii) Explain what effect the generation of the current has on the oscillation of the magnet. [2]

Part 2 Nuclear fusion

The diagram shows the variation of nuclear binding energy per nucleon with nucleon number for some of the lighter nuclides.
[Graph: binding energy per nucleon / MeV (0 to 10) against nucleon number (0 to 120); $^{2}_{1}$H at about 1.1 MeV, $^{4}_{2}$He at about 7.1 MeV, curve peaking near 8.8 MeV around nucleon number 60]

(a) (i) Outline, with reference to mass defect, what is meant by the term nuclear binding energy. [2]
(ii) Label, with the letter S, the region on the graph where nuclei are most stable. [1]
(iii) Show that the energy released when two $^{2}_{1}$H nuclei fuse to make a $^{4}_{2}$He nucleus is approximately 4 pJ. [4]

(b) In one nuclear reaction two deuterons (hydrogen-2) fuse to form tritium (hydrogen-3) and another particle. The tritium undergoes $\beta^-$ decay to form an isotope of helium.
(i) Identify the missing particles to complete the equations. [4]
$^{2}_{1}\text{H} + ^{2}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow ^{3}_{1}\text{H} + \ldots$

B3. This question is about alternative energy supplies.

A small island community requires a peak power of 850 kW. Two systems are available for supplying the energy: using wind power or photovoltaic cells.

(a) (i) Outline, with reference to the energy conversions in the machine, the main features of a conventional horizontal-axis wind generator. [3]
(ii) The mean wind speed on the island is 8.0 m s$^{-1}$. Show that the maximum power available from a wind generator of blade length 45 m is approximately 2 MW. [2]
Density of air = 1.2 kg m$^{-3}$
(iii) The efficiency of the generator is 24%. Deduce the number of these generators that would be required to provide the islanders with enough power to meet their energy requirements. [2]

(b) The graph below shows how the wind speed varies with height above the land and above the sea.
[Graph: height / m (0 to 160) against mean wind speed / m s$^{-1}$ (6 to 14); two curves, land and sea, sea curve at higher speeds]
(i) Suggest why, for any given height, the mean wind speed above the sea is greater than the mean wind speed above the land. [1]
(ii) There is a choice of mounting the wind generators either 60 m above the land or 60 m above the sea.
Calculate the ratio
$$\frac{\text{power available from a land-based generator}}{\text{power available from a sea-based generator}}$$
at a height of 60 m. [2]

(c) Distinguish between photovoltaic cells and solar heating panels. [2]

(d) The diagram shows 12 photovoltaic cells connected in series and in parallel to form a module to provide electrical power.
[Diagram: three parallel rows, each of four photovoltaic cells in series]
Each cell in the module has an emf of 0.75 V and an internal resistance of 1.8 Ω.
(i) Calculate the emf of the module. [1]
(ii) Determine the internal resistance of the module. [3]
(iii) The diagram below shows the module connected to a load resistor of resistance 2.2 Ω.
[Diagram: the module connected across a 2.2 Ω resistor]
Calculate the power dissipated in the load resistor. [2]
(iv) Discuss the benefits of having cells combined in series and parallel within the module. [2]

(e) The intensity of the Sun's radiation at the position of the Earth's orbit (the solar constant) is approximately $1.4 \times 10^{3}$ W m$^{-2}$.
(i) Explain why the average solar power per square metre arriving at the Earth is $3.5 \times 10^{2}$ W. [2]
(ii) State why the solar constant is an approximate value. [1]
(iii) Photovoltaic cells are approximately 20% efficient. Estimate the minimum area needed to supply an average power of 850 kW over a 24 hour period. [2]
